# On the Pleasure of Small Attentions

There's something worth noticing in the way light changes across an afternoon—how it starts sharp and white at noon, then slowly turns gold, then amber, then disappears into blue dusk without ever announcing the transitions. We rarely watch it happen in real time. We glance up, notice the quality has shifted, and wonder when that occurred.

I think a lot of life works this way. Change arrives gradually enough that we miss the mechanism, only the result. A skill improves, a relationship deepens or frays, a city becomes familiar—all through accumulation too slow to witness directly.

This makes me suspicious of the stories we tell about turning points. We like dramatic narratives: the day everything changed, the moment of realization. But maybe most transformation is quieter than that, less a lightning bolt and more like sediment settling, layer by layer, until one day you notice the riverbed has shifted.

There's a kind of humility in accepting this. It means less credit for sudden insight, less blame for sudden failure. It means the boring Tuesday afternoons matter as much as the dramatic ones—maybe more, since they're more numerous and their cumulative weight does most of the actual work.

I don't know if this is consoling or unsettling. Probably both. It suggests we have less control over our own becoming than we'd like to believe, but also that small, unremarkable efforts aren't wasted just because they don't feel significant in the moment. The light is changing right now. You just can't see it move.
